g.text: In 2PC phase 1 leaves transactions UNCOMMITTED. In TC/C it fully commits.
That one difference is why 2PC blocks on a coordinator crash and TC/C does not - nothing is ever held.
Before any protocol: the two orderings are NOT symmetric
system total $10 SHORT
DEBIT FIRST nobody can spend it. Recoverable.
system total $10 OVER
CREDIT FIRST C can spend $10 that A still has.
A temporary DEFICIT is recoverable; a temporary SURPLUS is exploitable. If both spend, the system has paid out money it never
had - a mint, and unrecoverable, because you cannot claw back a completed downstream payment.
The consequence people miss: this also FORBIDS running the two legs in parallel, since parallelism would create a window
where the credit might land first. A real latency cost paid for a correctness reason - and a constraint on ANY protocol you pick.
Phase 1, drawn three ways
2PC - rejected
PREPARE (A)
PREPARE (C)
LOCKS HELD, uncommitted
If the coordinator dies here, both participants sit with
prepared transactions and LOCKS HELD INDEFINITELY. They
cannot decide alone: committing risks a mint if the other
aborted, aborting risks losing a committed transfer. So a
prepared participant must BLOCK. Both accounts freeze,
and so does every transfer touching them.
TC/C - chosen
Try: A -= 10
Try: NOP on C
COMMITTED - nothing held
Each partition's local transaction begins and ends in
microseconds. A coordinator crash leaves NO ONE blocked -
just an unfinished transfer that a recovery worker drives
to a terminal state.
The cost: the intermediate state is VISIBLE.
Saga - the near-twin
T1: debit A
T2: credit C
strictly LINEAR
For two legs, near-identical to TC/C. TC/C wins on two
counts: its phases are PARALLELIZABLE (a 5-way split
payment confirms all five at once), and its Try phase
expresses RESERVATION - 'hold $10' is a weaker, useful
operation Saga has no vocabulary for.
What TC/C takes on in exchange
coordinator dies mid-transfer
A phase-status record is written BEFORE phase 1.
Without it an orphaned debit exists that nothing
knows to compensate. It is the recovery anchor.
a leg is retried and applied twice
Every leg carries (transaction_id, leg_number), and
the partition refuses one it has already applied.
Idempotency at the PARTITION, not just the API.
a Cancel arrives BEFORE its Try
The subtlest bug: the partition records an OUT-OF-ORDER
flag, and a later Try checks it and refuses. A tombstone
for an operation that has not happened yet.
Without the out-of-order flag: the Try is delayed, the deadline passes, recovery sends Cancel which arrives first and no-ops,
then the delayed Try lands and debits A - and NOTHING will ever compensate it. Money lost. Most TC/C write-ups omit this.
What we give up is ATOMICITY: a real millisecond window exists where the system's total is short. Three things make that
acceptable - the window is one partition round trip; debit-first makes it a deficit nobody can spend; and any global-sum audit
runs against the EVENT LOG at a committed sequence position, never a live scan of balances, so it never observes the window.
That third point is why TC/C and event sourcing belong together here rather than being two independent choices.
